title.en: Forces: hands-on activities from the textbook

text.en: Why do coins slide farther on a polished floor, and why does a chair move back when you push a table? Chapter 6's activities answer these.

Activity 6.1 stacks four coins and pushes them on level surfaces of different materials. The stack travels farthest on the smoothest surface.
Activity 6.2 pulls a wooden block with a spring balance. The reading when it just moves is an approximate measure of the force of friction, smallest on the surface where the coins went farthest.
If there were no friction a moving object would keep moving. This tendency to resist change in motion is inertia.
Activities 6.3 and 6.4 are teacher demonstrations with a cart pulled by a cup of weights. Doubling the mass of the cart while the force stays the same gives a smaller acceleration.
Activity 6.5 has you sit on a wheeled chair with legs raised and push a heavy table. You move backward as the table is pushed forward, showing equal and opposite reaction.
Activity 6.6 joins two identical spring balances by their hooks and pulls. Both read the same, showing action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude.
Activity 6.7 sends an inflated balloon along a thread with a straw. The air rushes backward and the balloon moves forward.
Together these activities support Newton's three laws of motion.

problem.en: Why does the balloon move forward when the air escapes backward?

text.en: The air pushes the balloon forward with an equal and opposite force.
So the balloon moves forward, which is how rockets work.

prompt.en: Describe how you could show Newton's third law at home.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the reaction acts on the same object

points.en: Friction is smaller on smooth surfaces, so objects travel farther.
Inertia is the tendency to resist change in motion.
For the same force a heavier cart accelerates less.
Action and reaction are equal and opposite on different objects.
